newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn hails summit, says Russia must be respected.
newsitem.headline: Bonn hails summit, says Russia must be respected.

text.p: BONN, March 22 (March) - Germany, Russia's closest western ally, on Saturday hailed the summit between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin as a success, but warned that an enlarged NATO must take Russian security interests seriously.

Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told German newspaper Express the two-day meeting that ended in Helsinki on Friday increased mutual trust between the former Cold War foes, but said new NATO members in east Europe should not be treated as inferior.

"No one expected that, after the summit, Russia would say: 'Yes indeed, we are in favour of NATO expansion'. The important thing is the ball is being played further ahead in the field," Kinkel told the Cologne-based newspaper in an interview.

Werner Hoyer, the State Secretary in the Foreign Ministry, told German radio no more progress in talks on NATO expansion could possibly have been expected and that Yeltsin could not have made further concessions because of huge pressure at home.

Hoyer said Russia had become a victim of its own propaganda that presented the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation as an aggressive alliance, adding: "That's why it was hard for Russia to make it round the corner".

Yeltsin agreed in Helsinki to sign a charter building a new relationship with NATO, despite Moscow's continued opposition to the eastward expansion of the alliance, and dropped a key Russian demand the charter should be legally binding.
He also promised to minimise differences with the West over NATO enlargement, drawing charges from communist opponents in the Russian parliament Moscow had caved in to shameful defeat.

Clinton pledged that east European countries would be able to join NATO as planned after the summit. The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are the leading candidates to be invited to join after an alliance summit in Madrid in July.

Both Kinkel and Hoyer said NATO wanted a new security order in which Russia was included as a partner. "We must take Russia's legitimate security interests seriously and act accordingly," Kinkel said.
